title: How do you deploy microservices to containers (Dockerfile, docker-compose, Kubernetes deployment, scaling)?
shortTitle: How do you deploy microservices to containers (Dockerfile, docker-compose, Kubernetes, scaling)

s1_definition.profdef: Deploying a microservice to containers means packaging the service and everything it needs to run into one immutable image with a Dockerfile, running that image as a container locally or in a group with docker-compose, and running it in production on an orchestrator like Kubernetes that schedules the container onto machines, keeps the desired number of copies alive, exposes it behind a stable network name, and scales the number of copies up and down based on load. The container gives identical behaviour on a laptop and in production because the image carries the exact runtime, and the orchestrator provides health checking, self-healing, rolling updates, and horizontal scaling.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of each service at National Bank of India as a specialised counter. A Dockerfile is the instruction sheet for building one fully-equipped portable counter, stocked with its exact tools, forms, and software, so it works the same wherever you drop it. docker-compose is how you set up a few such counters together on your own desk for testing, the transfer counter, its database, and a message queue, all wired up with one command. Kubernetes is the branch manager of a huge building: you tell it you want three transfer counters running at all times, and it finds space for them, replaces any that break, routes customers to healthy ones, and when the queue grows it opens more counters automatically and closes them when the rush ends.
s1_definition.oneliner: The Dockerfile builds one immutable image, docker-compose runs a small set of containers together for local development, and Kubernetes runs them in production with self-healing, rolling updates, and automatic horizontal scaling.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Deploying a microservice to containers means packaging the service and everything it needs to run into one immutable image with a Dockerfile, running that image as a container locally or in a group with docker-compose, and running it in production on an orchestrator like Kubernetes that schedules the container onto machines, keeps the desired number of copies alive, exposes it behind a stable network name, and scales the number of copies up and down based on load. The container gives identical behaviour on a laptop and in production because the image carries the exact runtime, and the orchestrator provides health checking, self-healing, rolling updates, and horizontal scaling.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of each service at National Bank of India as a specialised counter. A Dockerfile is the instruction sheet for building one fully-equipped portable counter, stocked with its exact tools, forms, and software, so it works the same wherever you drop it. docker-compose is how you set up a few such counters together on your own desk for testing, the transfer counter, its database, and a message queue, all wired up with one command. Kubernetes is the branch manager of a huge building: you tell it you want three transfer counters running at all times, and it finds space for them, replaces any that break, routes customers to healthy ones, and when the queue grows it opens more counters automatically and closes them when the rush ends.

**One line to remember:** The Dockerfile builds one immutable image, docker-compose runs a small set of containers together for local development, and Kubernetes runs them in production with self-healing, rolling updates, and automatic horizontal scaling.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the Dockerfile, because the image is the unit everything else builds on. A good Java service image is built in two stages to stay small and secure. The first stage uses a full JDK image to compile and package the application, and the second stage copies only the resulting jar into a slim JRE base image, so the runtime image does not carry the compiler or build tools. For example the build stage runs `mvn -q clean package -DskipTests` and the runtime stage does `COPY --from=build /app/target/transfer-service.jar app.jar` followed by `ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app.jar"]`. You run the container as a non-root user with `USER 1001`, you expose the port with `EXPOSE 8080`, and you pass configuration through environment variables rather than baking secrets into the image, which keeps the same image usable across dev, staging, and production.

The image must be immutable and self-contained, meaning the same image that passed tests is the exact one that runs in production, identified by a content digest or a version tag like `transfer-service:1.4.0`. You never edit a running container; to change anything you build a new image and roll it out. This is the core benefit over shipping a jar onto a hand-configured server, where environment drift causes the classic "works on my machine" failures.

docker-compose is for local development and simple multi-container setups. A `docker-compose.yml` declares several services, for example the transfer service, a PostgreSQL database, and a Kafka broker, with their images, ports, environment variables, volumes for data, and a dependency order with `depends_on`. One command, `docker compose up`, starts the whole local stack wired together on a private network where services reach each other by service name, so the transfer service connects to the database at host `postgres`. Compose is excellent for development and integration tests but is not a production orchestrator, because it has no real scheduling across many machines, limited self-healing, and no sophisticated rolling updates.

Kubernetes is the production orchestrator. You describe the desired state in YAML and Kubernetes continuously works to make reality match it. A Deployment declares which image to run and how many replicas you want, say `replicas: 3`, and Kubernetes creates three Pods, each a running container, spread across nodes. If a Pod crashes or a node dies, the Deployment notices the gap and starts a replacement, which is self-healing. A Service gives the set of Pods one stable virtual IP and DNS name, load-balancing requests across the healthy Pods, so callers never need to know individual Pod addresses. Configuration comes from ConfigMaps for non-secret settings and Secrets for credentials, injected as environment variables or mounted files, keeping config out of the image.

Health is central to Kubernetes behaviour, and this is where Spring Boot Actuator fits. A liveness probe asks "is this process healthy, or should it be killed and restarted?" and a readiness probe asks "is this instance ready to receive traffic yet?", which matters during startup and during warm-up. You point them at `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`. During a rolling update Kubernetes only sends traffic to Pods that pass readiness, so you upgrade with zero downtime: it starts new Pods, waits for them to become ready, then terminates old ones a few at a time, controlled by `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`. If the new version is bad you roll back to the previous ReplicaSet.

Scaling has two kinds. Horizontal scaling changes the number of Pods and is the default for stateless services; the HorizontalPodAutoscaler watches a metric such as CPU or a custom metric like requests per second and adjusts the replica count between a minimum and maximum, for example scaling from three to twenty Pods when CPU crosses seventy percent. Vertical scaling changes the CPU and memory given to each Pod through resource requests and limits. You always set requests, which the scheduler uses to place Pods, and limits, which cap usage; for a JVM you also size the heap relative to the memory limit so the container is not killed for exceeding memory. The cluster autoscaler adds or removes whole machines when Pods cannot be scheduled for lack of capacity.

Senior nuances worth mentioning: keep services stateless so any Pod can serve any request and scaling is trivial, and push state into databases, caches, and object storage. Use readiness gates and graceful shutdown, where the app finishes in-flight requests on `SIGTERM` within the termination grace period, so rolling updates do not drop transactions. Pin base images by digest and scan them for vulnerabilities. Set resource requests and limits deliberately, because missing them causes noisy-neighbour problems and unpredictable scheduling. Externalise all configuration and secrets, prefer a secrets manager over raw Kubernetes Secrets for sensitive banking credentials, and expose health, metrics, and tracing so the platform and your dashboards can see the service.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India deployed its transfer service by copying a jar onto a server and starting it by hand, and every environment behaved slightly differently, so a release that worked in testing failed in production because the Java version differed. This is exactly the problem a Dockerfile solves, by packaging the exact runtime and the application into one immutable image that behaves identically everywhere.

Problem 2 — Developers needed the transfer service, its database, and a message broker running together on their laptops to test, and setting that up manually was slow and error-prone. This is exactly what docker-compose solves, by declaring the whole local stack in one file and starting it with a single command.

Problem 3 — In production a single transfer-service instance crashed during the salary-day rush and took the service down, and there was no automatic recovery or scaling. This is exactly what a Kubernetes Deployment with multiple replicas, health probes, and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler solves, by keeping several copies alive, restarting failed ones, and adding copies when load rises.

Our mini-project is the transfer service made container-ready. The code shows the Spring Boot transfer logic with Actuator health exposed, then a multi-stage Dockerfile, a docker-compose file for local development with PostgreSQL, and Kubernetes manifests for a Deployment, a Service, and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler. The demo traces a transfer from Rajesh to Priya running inside a container.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the immutable image and tag it with a version
docker build -t registry.bank.in/transfer-service:1.4.0 .

# Run the whole local stack (service + postgres) for development
docker compose up --build

# Test the transfer running inside the container
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CUR3001","amount":50000}'

# Push the image, then deploy to Kubernetes
docker push registry.bank.in/transfer-service:1.4.0
kubectl apply -f k8s/

# Watch rollout, scaling, and health
kubectl rollout status deployment/transfer-service
kubectl get pods -l app=transfer-service
kubectl get hpa transfer-service
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer request of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), hitting the service that is running as three Pods in Kubernetes.

Step 1: The build pipeline runs `docker build`, which executes the Dockerfile. The build stage compiles the code and produces the jar; the runtime stage copies only that jar into a slim JRE image. The output is one immutable image tagged `transfer-service:1.4.0`. The source code stays on disk; the image is a new artifact.

Step 2: The image is pushed to the registry, then `kubectl apply -f k8s/` sends the desired state to Kubernetes. Kubernetes reads the Deployment, sees it wants three replicas of that image, and schedules three Pods onto nodes. The data here is the desired-state YAML; the result is three running containers.

Step 3: Each Pod starts the JVM. Kubernetes calls the readiness probe at `/actuator/health/readiness` and waits until it returns healthy before adding the Pod to the Service's load-balancing pool. Until then the Pod exists but receives no traffic.

Step 4: The client's POST request arrives at the Service's stable address. The Service load-balances it to one healthy Pod, say Pod 2. The request body is deserialized into a TransferRequest carrying from SAV2001, to CUR3001, amount fifty thousand.

Step 5: Inside that Pod the TransferController calls TransferService.transfer within a transaction. It loads Rajesh (balance one million) and Priya (balance two hundred fifty thousand) from PostgreSQL, calls debit on Rajesh reducing him to nine hundred fifty thousand, credit on Priya raising her to three hundred thousand, and saves both. The database is shared state outside the Pod, so any Pod could have done this identically.

Step 6: The transaction commits, the controller returns 201 Created, and the Service routes the response back to the client. The Pod remains stateless; nothing about this request is stored in the Pod itself.

Step 7: During the salary-day rush CPU across the Pods climbs past seventy percent. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler observes this and raises the replica count from three toward twenty. New Pods start, pass readiness, and begin taking traffic, spreading the load. When the rush ends the autoscaler scales back down.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:10:22 INFO    Pod transfer-service-2 readiness=UP, added to Service pool
2026-10-24 15:10:25 INFO    Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 completed
2026-10-24 15:10:25 INFO    Response 201 Created  SAV2001 balance=950000  CUR3001 balance=300000
2026-10-24 15:14:03 INFO    HPA scaled transfer-service 3 -> 9 replicas (cpu 82%)
```

```
    │ HTTPS
    ▼
  Kubernetes Service (stable DNS: transfer-service)
    │ load-balances across READY Pods only
    ├───────────────┬───────────────┐
    ▼               ▼               ▼
  Pod 1           Pod 2 ◀ picked   Pod 3        ← Deployment replicas=3
  (ready)         (ready)          (ready)
                    │
                    ▼
  TransferController → TransferService (@Transactional)
    │ accountRepo.findById("SAV2001") → Rajesh  balance=1,000,000
    │ accountRepo.findById("CUR3001") → Priya   balance=250,000
    │ rajesh.debit(50000)  → 1,000,000 → 950,000
    │ priya.credit(50000)  → 250,000   → 300,000
    │ save both
    ▼
  PostgreSQL (shared state outside the Pods)
    │ COMMIT
    ▼
  Response: 201 Created {"status":"COMPLETED"}

  ── Under load ──
  HPA watches CPU ──→ 82% > 70% ──→ scale Deployment 3 → 9 Pods
  new Pods start → pass readiness → Service adds them to the pool
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Deploying a microservice to containers is a progression from one image to a production orchestrator, and I describe it in three steps. The Dockerfile packages the service and its exact runtime into one immutable image, and I build it in two stages so the runtime image carries only a slim JRE and the jar, not the compiler, I run it as a non-root user, and I pass configuration and secrets through environment variables instead of baking them in. The key property is that the same image that passed tests is the exact one that runs in production, identified by a version tag or digest, which eliminates the environment drift that causes works-on-my-machine failures.

For local development I use docker-compose, which declares the service together with its database and message broker in one file and starts the whole stack with a single command on a private network where services reach each other by name. It is ideal for development and integration tests, but it is not a production orchestrator because it has no real scheduling across machines, limited self-healing, and no sophisticated rolling updates.

In production I run on Kubernetes, where I declare desired state and the platform makes reality match it. A Deployment keeps a set number of replica Pods alive and self-heals by replacing any that die, a Service gives those Pods one stable name and load-balances across the healthy ones, and ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration without touching the image. Liveness and readiness probes, which I wire to Spring Boot Actuator, let Kubernetes restart unhealthy Pods and only send traffic to ready ones, which is what makes rolling updates zero-downtime. Scaling is mostly horizontal through the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, which watches a metric like CPU or requests per second and adjusts the replica count between a minimum and maximum, while resource requests and limits size each Pod and the cluster autoscaler adds machines when needed.

On my project at National Bank of India the transfer service was once a jar copied onto a server, and a release failed in production because the Java version differed from testing. We containerised it, used docker-compose so developers could run the service with its database locally, and deployed to Kubernetes with three replicas, Actuator-backed probes, and an autoscaler from three to twenty Pods. On the next salary-day rush CPU crossed seventy percent and Kubernetes scaled us out automatically and scaled back down afterwards, with no downtime during the upgrade because readiness gating meant only warmed-up Pods took traffic. The nuances I stress are keeping services stateless so any Pod can serve any request, implementing graceful shutdown so rolling updates do not drop in-flight transfers, and always setting resource requests and limits so one Pod cannot starve its neighbours.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that the Dockerfile builds one immutable image, docker-compose runs a small set of containers together for local development, and Kubernetes runs them in production with self-healing Deployments, stable Services, probe-driven zero-downtime rollouts, and automatic horizontal scaling, with the whole thing working only because the services are stateless and all state lives in the database and cache.

---

keyPoints: Horizontal scaling: add more instances behind load balancer
Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits
Auto-scaling: based on CPU, memory, request rate metrics
Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
